title: Hawkins v. McGee
summary: A physician’s sufficiently definite guarantee can create a contractual obligation. Compensation measures the promised result against the actual result, subject to the limits explained in the opinion.
notes:
Court: Supreme Court of New Hampshire (1929).

C&M pp. 2–3 contain the promise analysis; pp. 11–13 contain the damages analysis. The editors’ later statutory-override example on p. 4 concerns another jurisdiction and another case. It does not retroactively change the holding in Hawkins.

The graft of chest skin caused thick hair to grow on Hawkins's palm, which is why the case is known as the "hairy hand" case (Hawkins v. McGee, 84 N.H. 114, 146 A. 641 (1929)).

Procedural detail: the jury found for Hawkins, but the trial court set the verdict aside as excessive when Hawkins refused to accept a remittitur to $500, and the Supreme Court's ruling on the damages instruction sent the case back for a new trial.

sections.Parties: Hawkins, the patient, sought recovery from McGee, the physician who operated on his hand. The dispute concerns an alleged promise of a particular result, alongside the background possibility of a malpractice claim.
sections.Material Facts:
Hawkins’s right palm contained substantial scar tissue from an electrical burn about nine years earlier. McGee proposed removing the scar tissue and grafting skin from Hawkins’s chest. Before surgery, the physician estimated a short hospital stay and recovery period. More importantly, witnesses attributed to him a guarantee of a “hundred per cent perfect” or good hand. Hawkins was present when the guarantee was allegedly made.

The context mattered as much as the strength of those words. There was evidence that McGee repeatedly sought permission from Hawkins’s father to perform the operation. The patient’s lawyer suggested that the doctor wanted experience in skin grafting. That evidence could support the inference that the assurance was intended to induce consent to surgery. The opinion does not turn the lawyer’s suggested motive into an independently established medical fact.
sections.Procedural History: The contract question was submitted to the jury. The challenged damages instruction allowed compensation for surgical pain and for worsening of the hand beyond its preoperative condition. The New Hampshire Supreme Court held that the alleged guarantee could properly be considered by the jury but found the damages instruction erroneous. The casebook reports that the court ordered a new trial. The two assigned excerpts address these separate questions; the malpractice disposition is mentioned in the later Sullivan discussion.
sections.Issue: Could the doctor’s words, understood in their context, amount to a promise of a guaranteed result? If so, should damages restore the patient’s preoperative position or compensate him for the difference between the hand promised and the hand produced?
sections.Holding: The evidence permitted the jury to find the alleged guarantee. The correct contract measure was the difference between the value to Hawkins of the promised good hand and the actual hand, together with qualifying incidental consequences. Ordinary pain necessarily associated with the agreed surgery was not a separate item of expectation damages.
sections.Reasoning:
The court distinguished statements about the likely duration of treatment from the specific assurance of a perfect result. The former were predictions; the latter could be understood as a commitment, particularly when coupled with repeated solicitation of consent. The trial judge first had to decide whether the words were capable of carrying the contractual meaning asserted. The jury could then decide whether that promise was made.

For damages, the court asked what Hawkins would have had if McGee had performed the promise. Ordinary surgical pain would have occurred even with successful performance, so it was part of what Hawkins undertook to bear for the promised improvement. A separate award for worsening also used the wrong benchmark: the difference between the promised and actual hand already accounts for deterioration, and breach could occur even if the operation merely failed to improve the hand. The court also rejected a proposed instruction requiring proof that another operation could not correct the condition, noting the physician’s refusal to perform one.

priorVersions.summary: A surgeon’s specific guarantee may be a contractual promise. The remedy measures the promised hand against the hand actually delivered.
priorVersions.notes:
Court: Supreme Court of New Hampshire (1929).

Reading distinction: the casebook uses the same case to introduce both the identification of an enforceable promise and the expectation measure. Contractual liability for a promised result and negligence in providing medical care are separate questions. The surrounding notes ask how later medical-promise formalities and the context of reassurance affect enforcement; they are not part of this case’s holding.

sections.Parties: George Hawkins, the patient, sued Dr. McGee, the surgeon. The defendant challenged the contract claim and the damages instructions.
sections.Material Facts: Hawkins had a scarred right hand from an electrical burn suffered years earlier. McGee solicited the operation and grafted skin from Hawkins’s chest onto the hand. Hawkins offered evidence of a guarantee of a “hundred per cent perfect” or “hundred per cent good” hand. Hair grew on the graft. Statements predicting a three- or four-day hospital stay and an early return to work were also in evidence.
sections.Procedural History: The casebook splits one decision into a liability excerpt and a damages excerpt. In the first, the court treats the guarantee as evidence that could go to a jury, while treating the recovery-time statements as estimates. In the later excerpt, it rejects the trial court’s damages instruction and orders a new trial. The assigned text does not establish a final recovery after that new trial.
sections.Issue: Could the surgeon’s words reasonably amount to a promise of a specified result, and how should damages for its breach be measured?
sections.Holding: The asserted guarantee could support a contract finding. Damages are the difference between the value of the hand as promised and its value as delivered, together with qualifying incidental consequences. Ordinary pain inherent in the contemplated operation is excluded from that calculation.
sections.Reasoning: The court first decides whether words can reasonably bear the alleged contractual meaning; where they can, the jury determines whether they were used and understood that way. The surgeon’s solicitation and interest in undertaking the operation give context to the guarantee. The damages comparison places Hawkins in the position successful performance would have produced. Ordinary operative pain was part of the performance Hawkins agreed to undergo, rather than an additional loss caused by failure to produce the promised result. Worsening is already captured in the difference between the actual and promised hand and should not be counted twice.

learning.why: This case begins the course’s two recurring inquiries: what obligation was undertaken, and what the law will do when it is not performed. Keep the formation ruling separate from the correction of the damages instruction.

topics.promises: The language and context distinguish a guarantee from a prediction.
topics.assent: The doctor’s objectively communicated commitment could induce consent.
topics.expectation: The promised result supplies the damages benchmark.
topics.remedies: The two excerpts connect recognition of a promise to the remedy for its breach.
topics.promise-or-prediction: The threshold issue was whether the surgeon's words were a contractual guarantee or merely a prediction or expression of opinion about the operation's outcome.
topics.reliance-interest: The court's refusal to award pain and suffering as an item of damages illustrates the line between reliance-type losses and the expectation measure it adopted.
